title: Optimize query performance for Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL

questions.q: Which index type does a query that uses ST_DISTANCE to find nearby points of interest need?

options.why: Correct. Spatial indexes support ST_DISTANCE, ST_WITHIN and ST_INTERSECTS.
Composite indexes handle multi-property sorting and filters.
Range indexes handle equality, ranges and single-property ORDER BY.
Vector indexes support VectorDistance.

questions.hint: Distance between coordinates needs a geography-aware index.
questions.explain: Pick the index type by the query function: spatial for geo, vector for similarity.

questions.q: What is the default indexing mode for a new Cosmos DB container?

options.why: Lazy is deprecated and new containers can't use it.
Correct. Consistent updates indexes synchronously with each write and is the default.
None disables indexing.
Eventual is a consistency level, not an indexing mode.

questions.hint: The default mode updates indexes in step with every write.
questions.explain: Consistent mode keeps queries in step with committed writes.

questions.q: Which path indexes only the scalar value of a top-level property named title?

options.why: /[] indexes array elements.
That isn't valid index path syntax.
/* indexes everything under the path.
Correct. /? indexes the scalar value at the property.

questions.hint: A path ending in /? means just this value. /* means everything below it.
questions.explain: /? = scalar, /[] = array elements, /* = everything under the path.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A container uses partition key `/tenantId` and a selective policy with `/*` in excludedPaths.

rows.text: The tenantId path is indexed automatically anyway.
rows.why: The partition key isn't indexed automatically unless it's /id; include it explicitly.

rows.text: id and _ts remain indexed even though /* is excluded.
rows.why: id and _ts are always indexed in consistent mode.

rows.text: With /* excluded, every property is still range-indexed by default.
rows.why: Excluding /* means only explicitly included paths (plus id and _ts) are indexed.

rows.text: If /* is excluded and /title/? is included, title is indexed because the more specific path wins.
rows.why: The more specific path takes precedence.

questions.hint: id and _ts are always indexed. Excluding /* means you must opt in to everything else.
questions.explain: Selective policies must explicitly include every queried property, including the partition key.

questions.q: A container is used only as a key-value store: items are read by id and partition key, and bulk writes must be as fast as possible. Which indexing mode fits?

options.why: Consistent adds index work to each write you don't need here.
Lazy is deprecated and unavailable for new containers.
id and _ts are always indexed in consistent mode anyway, so this still maintains indexes.
Correct. None treats the container as a pure key-value store and can speed up bulk writes.

questions.hint: No queries except point reads, and writes must be fast. Indexing can be switched off entirely.
questions.explain: Use none only when you never query by secondary properties; queries would otherwise do full scans.

questions.q: An old container still uses the lazy indexing mode, and a teammate wants to create a new container with the same setting. What should you tell them?

options.text: Lazy indexing works only with shared database throughput
options.why: Throughput mode isn't the issue. Lazy indexing is deprecated.

options.text: Lazy indexing is deprecated: new containers can't use it, and existing ones should move to consistent
options.why: Correct. Lazy mode is deprecated, so migrate existing containers to consistent.

options.text: Lazy indexing is the recommended mode for AI workloads with heavy writes
options.why: Lazy mode is deprecated. For write-heavy key-value use, Learn discusses the none mode.

options.text: Lazy indexing is the default for containers created from the portal
options.why: The default indexing mode is consistent.

questions.hint: One of the indexing modes is no longer offered.
questions.explain: Azure Cosmos DB previously supported lazy indexing. It's deprecated: new containers can't use it, and existing containers with lazy indexing should migrate to consistent mode.

questions.q: A query runs `ORDER BY c.relevanceScore DESC, c.uploadDate DESC` and fails with an error. What does it need?

options.text: A range index on relevanceScore and another on uploadDate
options.why: ORDER BY on two properties needs a composite index, not a single range index.

options.text: A composite index (relevanceScore DESC, uploadDate DESC)
options.why: Correct. The composite index must match the property sequence and directions.

options.text: A tuple index covering both of the sorted properties
options.why: Tuple indexes are for properties inside array elements.

options.text: A spatial index on uploadDate for the date sort
options.why: Spatial indexes are for geospatial functions.

questions.hint: Sorting on two properties needs one index that covers both, in that order.
questions.explain: Multi-property ORDER BY requires a matching composite index.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A container has one composite index: `(relevanceScore DESC, uploadDate DESC)`.

rows.text: It serves ORDER BY c.relevanceScore ASC, c.uploadDate ASC.
rows.why: Composite indexes support the exact opposite order on all paths.

rows.text: It serves ORDER BY c.relevanceScore DESC, c.uploadDate ASC.
rows.why: Mixed orders need a separate composite index.

rows.text: It serves ORDER BY c.uploadDate DESC, c.relevanceScore DESC.

questions.hint: A composite index serves its exact order and the full reverse, and nothing else.
questions.explain: Same sequence; same directions or the exact reverse.

questions.q: A query filters `category = 'reports' AND department = 'finance' AND createdDate > '2024-06-01'`. How should the composite index be ordered?

options.why: Correct. Equality filters first, the single range filter last.
The range filter must be last.
The range filter can't be in the middle.

options.text: A single range index on createdDate
options.why: A single range index doesn't optimize the combined filter as well.

questions.hint: Equality filters first, the range filter last.
questions.explain: Place equality filters first; each composite index supports one range filter, and it goes last.

questions.q: You're replacing composite index X with a better composite index Y on a busy container with millions of items. What order of steps keeps queries supported?

options.text: Switch indexing mode to none, then add Y afterward
options.why: Mode none disables indexing entirely.

options.text: Add Y and remove X together in one policy update
options.why: X would stop being used immediately while Y is still being built.

options.text: Remove X first, then add Y in a second update
options.why: Removing X takes effect immediately, so queries scan until Y is built.

options.text: Add Y, wait for the transformation, then remove X
options.why: Correct. Add the new index first, wait, then remove the old one.

questions.hint: Removing an index takes effect at once. Adding one takes effect only after the transformation.
questions.explain: Added indexes help only after transformation; removed ones stop being used right away.

questions.q: Documents store chunks as an array of objects with position and tokens. Queries filter on both properties within the same chunk. Which path improves this?

options.why: Those paths aren't array-element paths.
Correct. A tuple index indexes the property combination within each array element.
/chunks/* indexes everything separately, not the combination per element.
Composite indexes on top-level paths don't index combinations inside array elements.

questions.hint: Indexing several properties of the same array element uses a special path syntax.
questions.explain: Tuple indexes suit chunked documents filtered on chunk position, size or other metadata.

questions.q: You added a composite index to a container with millions of items an hour ago, but the slow query costs the same RUs. Nothing else changed. What's the most likely reason?

options.text: Composite indexes don't reduce RU cost
options.why: They do once they're built and match the query.

options.text: The index transformation hasn't finished, so queries can't use the new index yet
options.why: Correct. Index changes apply asynchronously, and new indexes help only after the transformation completes.

options.text: The query must name the index in a hint
options.why: Cosmos DB picks indexes automatically. There's no index hint to add.

options.text: The container needs a restart before new indexes load
options.why: Cosmos DB containers aren't restarted. The transformation runs in the background.

questions.hint: Changing an indexing policy starts background work. Can large containers take hours?
questions.explain: Index changes run as an asynchronous transformation. New indexes don't improve queries until it completes, which can take hours on large containers. Track progress in the portal or CLI.

questions.q: You upgrade from a 1,536-dimension embedding model to text-embedding-3-large (3,072 dimensions). What must you do in Cosmos DB?

options.text: Create a new container with an updated vector policy and migrate
options.why: Correct. Different dimensions require a new container and data migration.
Index tuning doesn't change the policy's dimensions.

options.text: Edit the dimensions in the existing vector policy
options.why: Vector policies can't be modified after creation.

options.text: Change the vector index type to flat
options.why: flat supports at most 505 dimensions.

questions.hint: The vector embedding policy can't change after the container is created.
questions.explain: Plan dimensions, data type and distance function up front; vector policies are immutable.

questions.q: Users always filter by category first, and each category holds a few hundred 384-dimension vectors. They want exact results. Which vector index fits?

options.why: Correct. Flat gives exact results and works well when filters shrink the candidate set (and 384 ≤ 505 dims).
diskANN is approximate and aimed at large datasets.
quantizedFlat trades slight accuracy for speed.
Without a vector index, similarity queries scan everything; flat is the right index here.

questions.hint: Small, pre-filtered sets and exact results: brute force over few vectors is fine.
questions.explain: Flat indexes suit small candidate sets and exact-accuracy needs.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A team tunes a diskANN index on a large embedding collection.

rows.text: Raising indexingSearchListSize can improve index quality but slows index builds.
rows.why: Higher values improve quality and accuracy but take longer to build.

rows.text: indexingSearchListSize also applies to quantizedFlat indexes.
Most applications perform well with the default parameters.
rows.why: Tune only if you observe accuracy issues or need specific latency targets.

rows.text: indexingSearchListSize can be set as high as 5,000.

questions.hint: Most apps need no tuning. A bigger search list means better quality but slower builds, and it applies to diskANN.
questions.explain: Defaults are usually fine; quantizationByteSize applies to both, indexingSearchListSize only to diskANN.

questions.q: Search quality on a quantizedFlat index is slightly below target, and the team can accept more storage. Which vector index setting should they raise?

options.text: The policy's dimensions, above the model's output size
options.why: Dimensions must match the embedding model.
Partitions don't control how much vectors are compressed.
indexingSearchListSize is a diskANN setting.
Correct. Larger values keep more information, which improves accuracy at the cost of storage and possibly throughput.

questions.hint: Quantization compresses vectors. Which setting controls how much is kept?
questions.explain: quantizationByteSize controls how much compression is applied. Larger values preserve more information and improve accuracy, with more storage and possibly lower throughput. The default is chosen dynamically.

questions.q: Query metrics show 48,000 retrieved documents and 25 output documents for a frequent query. What does this suggest?

options.text: Filtering is inefficient, so an index is likely missing
options.why: Correct. A high retrieved-to-output ratio points to inefficient filtering; check indexes.

options.text: The container has too many vector indexes
options.why: Vector indexes don't cause scans of metadata filters.

options.text: The query uses too strong a consistency level
options.why: Consistency affects replica reads, not this ratio.

options.text: The partition key has too many distinct values
options.why: High cardinality is good for partition keys.

questions.hint: Many documents read but few returned means the filter isn't using an index.
questions.explain: Use index utilization and retrieved vs output counts to find missing indexes.

questions.q: An IoT ingestion pipeline writes thousands of documents per second and queries them once a day for a report. What indexing strategy fits?

options.text: Index every property with /* and add many composite indexes
options.why: Every index raises write latency and RUs.

options.text: Index minimally: only the few properties the daily query needs
options.why: Correct. Write-heavy workloads benefit from minimal indexing.

options.text: Switch to bounded staleness to reduce write cost
options.why: Consistency doesn't change write RU cost per operation.

options.text: Use comprehensive composite indexes because AI apps are read-heavy
options.why: This workload is write-heavy, not read-heavy.

questions.hint: Heavy writes and rare reads: every indexed path costs on each write.
questions.explain: Write-heavy → minimal indexes; read-heavy → comprehensive indexes.

questions.q: A document has title, documentType, category, uploadDate, a large content field, summary and an embedding. Queries filter on documentType, category and uploadDate and show content and summary. Which two belong in the indexing policy? (Select two.)

options.why: content is only displayed; don't index it.
Correct. documentType is filtered, so index it.
summary is only displayed; don't index it.
Correct. Embedding search uses a vector index, not a range index.

questions.hint: Index what you filter on, exclude what you only display, and give the embedding a vector index.
questions.explain: Index the properties used in queries plus a vector index; exclude display-only fields.

questions.q: Query metrics show a high ratio of retrieved to output documents for a frequent query. You add the missing index. What should you do next, following Learn's workflow?

options.text: Immediately remove the old indexes to save write RUs
options.why: Removing indexes too early can make other queries fall back to scans.

options.text: Wait for the transformation to complete, then measure the query's RU cost again
options.why: Correct. Create the index, wait for the transformation, then measure again to confirm the improvement.

options.text: Switch the account to strong consistency to make the index take effect
options.why: Consistency doesn't control when indexes take effect.

options.text: Recreate the container so that the index applies to existing items
options.why: Policy changes transform existing data in the background. You don't need a new container.

questions.hint: An index change isn't instant. What proves it worked?
questions.explain: When metrics show low index utilization or high retrieved-to-output ratios, add or modify indexes, wait for the transformation to complete, and measure query costs again.

questions.q: A user uploads a document and immediately searches for it in the same app. Which consistency level does Learn recommend for this read-your-writes need?

options.why: Correct. Session guarantees read-your-writes within the session.
Strong works but doubles read RUs and adds latency; Session is the recommended balance.
Eventual may return stale data with no ordering.
Consistent prefix guarantees order, not freshness.

questions.hint: The user needs to see their own write right away.
questions.explain: Session suits most AI apps: users see their own uploads immediately.

questions.q: Which consistency levels read from two replicas and cost about twice the read RUs?

options.why: These read from one replica.
Correct. Strong and bounded staleness read from two replicas (minority quorum).
These read from one replica.
Eventual reads from one replica.

questions.hint: Two levels read from two replicas.
questions.explain: Strong and bounded staleness reads cost 2×; the other levels 1×.

questions.q: Put the five Cosmos DB consistency levels in order from strongest to weakest.
questions.hint: From the strongest guarantee down to the weakest.
questions.explain: Stronger levels give fresher reads at the cost of latency, availability and (for the top two) read RUs.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. An upload service writes a document, and a separate search service queries it for the same user, both using Session consistency.

rows.text: The search service sees the new document only if it receives the session token from the upload.
rows.why: Across services you must pass session tokens explicitly.

rows.text: Session tokens are global and work for every partition.
Writes under Session consistency cost more RUs than under Eventual.
rows.why: Write RU costs don't vary by consistency level.

questions.hint: Session guarantees follow the session token, and they apply per partition.
questions.explain: Pass session tokens between services that handle the same user flow.

questions.q: A globally distributed app uses multiple write regions and asks for Strong consistency for payment records. What should you know?

options.text: Strong costs the same read RUs as Session
options.why: Strong reads cost 2× because they read from two replicas.

options.text: Strong guarantees reads at most K versions behind
options.why: That describes bounded staleness.

options.text: Strong isn't supported with multiple write regions
options.why: Correct. Strong consistency with multiple write regions isn't supported.

options.text: Strong reads from a single replica
options.why: Strong reads from two replicas.

questions.hint: One consistency level can't work with multiple write regions.
questions.explain: For multi-region writes, choose Session or weaker; Strong needs a single write region.

questions.q: An analytics job uses Eventual consistency. PBS metrics show it returns the latest data 99.6% of the time. What does Learn suggest?

options.text: Move to bounded staleness to reduce read RUs
options.why: Bounded staleness reads cost 2×, so it raises RUs.

options.text: Switch the job to Strong to remove the remaining 0.4%
options.why: Strong doubles read RUs; analytics rarely needs it.

options.text: PBS measures Session reads, so ignore it here
options.why: PBS measures how often eventual reads return the latest data.

options.text: Eventual is probably safe for more operations
options.why: Correct. If PBS shows current data more than 99% of the time, you might use eventual for more operations.

questions.hint: Probabilistic bounded staleness shows how often weaker reads are already up to date.
questions.explain: Use PBS metrics (Metrics → Consistency) to validate weaker consistency choices.
